claims.text: A threshold concentration of a protective oxide-forming element exists in high-entropy alloys.
Reaching this threshold promotes preferential segregation of the protective element to the surface during high-temperature exposure.
Surface segregation of the protective element enables formation and stabilization of a continuous, slow-growing protective oxide layer.
A continuous protective oxide layer such as alumina dramatically reduces oxidation kinetics relative to alloys containing less of the protective element.
The starting alloy composition is uniformly distributed before high-temperature exposure.
Exposure above approximately 800°C provides sufficient oxidation kinetics for the proposed comparison.
The protective oxide scale acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
Above the protective-element threshold, alloys form a coherent and stable oxide scale that limits further oxidation.
Below the protective-element threshold, alloys form discontinuous or porous oxide scales that permit more rapid oxidative degradation.
Alloys above the threshold will have lower mass gain than alloys below the threshold.
Alloys above the threshold will develop thinner and more uniform oxide layers than alloys below the threshold.
The proposed mechanism applies under high-temperature oxidizing conditions when the selected protective oxide-forming element has a dominant role.
Competing oxide-forming elements or temperatures outside the stated range may change the behavior.
The effective concentration threshold and segregation kinetics vary with alloy system and processing history.
A controlled comparison should vary protective-element concentration across the proposed threshold while otherwise holding processing and exposure conditions constant.
Failure of the higher-concentration alloy to produce a more continuous, uniform, slower-growing scale and lower oxidation rate than the lower-concentration alloy would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The design says to vary the concentration of one element while keeping all other alloying elements constant or making samples otherwise identical. For normalized alloy compositions, changing one element's atomic fraction necessarily changes at least one other element's fraction unless a balancing-element or substitution scheme is specified.
